name: Victor Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm assistant manager on Hollin Estate, about 900 hectares of wheat, oilseed rape and beans, plus 700 ewes. It's owned by a pension fund and run by a management company, so I answer to a manager who visits twice a month. My day is half outside with the team of five, half in the farm office sorting spray records, orders and rotas.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Outside, easily. Lambing and harvest are when I feel useful, and the team is good, especially Dorota, who's been shepherding longer than I've been alive. The office half is fine, and lately I've been asking a chatbot to draft the spray records, then checking them, which saves me maybe an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's roughly where I'd bet it ends up, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool and not much more, which is how I already use it. To the team I'd say nothing changes, and I'd mean it. Online I don't post much, maybe a shrug in the farm managers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means things stay as they are, and they're good. I earn well for a farm job, Sam's teaching salary is steady, and we've got about ten months saved plus our flat. My worry here is the pension fund itself, because every year they want a better return from the same land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the drafting trick for spray records and maybe try it for the lambing rota. I'd keep putting money into savings like we do. And I'd keep pushing the estate manager for a pay rise for Dorota, who's underpaid for what she knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the whole AI story, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pension fund wants more every year. What does that look like on the ground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they cut the hedge-laying budget and asked us to run the same flock with one fewer person at lambing. We managed, but we were all wrecked by April. AI not changing much doesn't change them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that pressure a threat to your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'm the one they rely on to make the numbers work. The threat is to the team around me. The owners of Hollin Estate have never once stood in a lambing shed at two in the morning.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool**, not much more, in the managers' forum.
I'd tell the team plainly that **nothing changes** for them.
think: Privately I think my job and **household money** are secure.
My real pressure is the **pension fund** squeezing more from the same land.
do: Keep using a chatbot to draft **spray records**, and try the **lambing rota**.
Keep adding to **savings** at the usual monthly rate.
Keep pressing the estate manager for **Dorota's pay rise**.
feel: He feels **calm**, and slightly **bored** by the AI story.
S0.quote: The owners of Hollin Estate have never once stood in a lambing shed at two in the morning.
fieldNote: His frustration is with **absentee owners**, not with technology.
He already uses AI **lightly** and checks its output himself.
He sees the **team**, not himself, as exposed to cost cutting.
Two steady incomes and owned **flat** make him genuinely secure.

steps.text: Keep the team and lambing routine as it is
Try the chatbot for drafting next spring's lambing rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's more real. The office half of my job is exactly that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should get the tools in, but on our terms, with the time saved going back into the land and the people. I'd say it in the union branch too, because I joined last year after the lambing cuts. Farm work isn't going anywhere yet, and I'd say that clearly so people don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the management company would try to merge assistant manager jobs across two or three estates. Ordering, records and planning would be done by software, and they'd keep one person to walk the fields. I'd probably be that person, but I'd be stretched across more land for the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the farm-management software properly in the first six months, before they bring it in, so I'm the one who sets it up. I'd raise a union claim that any merged roles get paid more, not the same. And I'd put an extra few hundred a month aside in case it goes badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, but I'd be watching the emails from head office very closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Dorota, nobody else can do what she does with sheep. I'd worry about Kieran, who's 23 and does a lot of the tractor and loader work, because self-driving tractors are the first thing they'd try. I'd want him on a mechanics course before that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the software early and also fight the merger. Isn't that a bit of both sides?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm fine with that. If the farm software is coming anyway, I'd rather be the person who knows it than the person it's done to. You can push for fair pay and still be good at your job.

say: I'd say bring in tools **on our terms**, with time saved going to people.
I'd tell the **union branch** that farm work isn't disappearing yet.
think: Privately I expect the company to **merge manager roles** across estates.
I'd likely keep a job but cover **more land** for the same pay.
do: Learn the **farm-management software** within six months, before rollout.
Raise a **union claim** for higher pay in any merged role.
Save a few **hundred extra** each month as a buffer.
feel: He feels **uneasy** and watchful about **head office** emails.
S1.quote: If the farm software is coming anyway, I'd rather be the person who knows it than the person it's done to.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking half** of his job as the part at risk.
He comfortably holds **two strategies**: learn early and bargain hard.
He worries for **Kieran**, the young tractor driver, ahead of himself.
His union membership grew out of real **lambing cuts**, not ideology alone.

steps.text: Learn the farm-management software in six months, before the rollout
File a union claim for higher pay in merged manager roles
Add a few hundred extra to savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a different conversation. Two years for the office, five for the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to step in, with income support and public ownership of some of this technology. At work I'd tell the team straight that I don't know what Hollin will look like, and I won't pretend to. I'd want the union pushing for a deal before the robots arrive, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 my office half is gone overnight, and the pension fund won't pay a manager's salary for someone who just walks fields. I'd guess they'd keep me on less money as the person who watches the machines, then by 2031 maybe not even that. With Sam's salary and our savings we'd manage a few years, but I can't see what I'd be doing at 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the agricultural robotics certificate at the college straight away, evening classes, because the people who fix and supervise farm robots will last longest. I'd hold off on trying for a baby, which Sam and I had planned for 2028. And I'd push hard through the union for a redundancy deal tied to years of service, not just a month's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got some control, but not much, and that's new for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam actually say about the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably say wait a year and see, and then argue about whether waiting even helps. Sam would say kids still need teachers, so her job is the steadier one. I'd feel bad that my plan for our family depended on a farm I don't own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if your pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car and the holiday in Portugal we do every September. We've got no debt apart from a small bit on the flat, so we'd pay that off fast. After that, it's just being careful.

say: I'd call for **income support** and some **public ownership** of the technology.
I'd tell the team honestly that I **don't know** Hollin's future.
think: Privately I expect my **office half** gone by 2028 and a **pay cut**.
By 2031 I may lose the **field role** too, and can't picture age 32.
do: Enrol in the **agricultural robotics** evening certificate straight away.
Delay **trying for a baby**, which was planned for 2028.
Push the union for a **redundancy deal** tied to years of service.
feel: He feels **anxious**, with less **control** than he's used to.
S2.quote: I'd feel bad that my plan for our family depended on a farm I don't own.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** matters to him: office goes first, fieldwork follows.
He chooses **robot maintenance** training as the longest-lasting role.
AGI reaches into **family plans**; the baby decision gets delayed.
Strong savings and **Sam's salary** keep him anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's agricultural robotics evening certificate
Put off trying for a baby until the farm job settles
Push the union for redundancy pay tied to years of service
Drop the second car and the September holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually get ready, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things about public support, but I'd also say it loudly to young farmers: start learning the machines now. In the forum I'd probably post a list of courses. I'd be calmer and more practical about it than in the fast version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I can be the robot person before anyone else at Hollin is. If I've got the certificate and a couple of years using the software, I'm the one they keep in 2034. I'm not thrilled about watching machines do lambing, but I'd rather be there than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robotics certificate next autumn, not straight away, so I can do it properly over two years. I'd use AI tools every week in the office instead of now and then, to get properly good at them. And we'd keep the baby plan, maybe a year later than we said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still a big change, but it feels like something I can walk through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the estate to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd ask the union to make it a standard request for every farm worker, not just managers. Dorota would never do it, she'd rather retire, and that's her right. Kieran, I'd drag along with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about the slower version harder than the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a way, yes. In the fast version you just react, but in the slower version you have to decide, and you can get it wrong. If I'd bet on robots and they arrived late, I'd have spent two years of evenings on nothing.

say: I'd tell young farmers to **learn the machines** now, while there's time.
I'd post a practical list of **courses** in the managers' forum.
think: Privately five years lets me become Hollin's **robot person** first.
I'd rather **supervise** machines at lambing than be gone.
do: Start the **robotics certificate** next autumn and finish over two years.
Use AI tools **weekly** in the farm office to build skill.
Keep the **baby plan**, pushed back about a year.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but able to **walk through** the change.
S3.quote: In the fast version you just react, but in the slower version you have to decide, and you can get it wrong.
fieldNote: More time shifts him from bargaining towards **planned retraining**.
He sees **decision risk** in the slow scenario that the fast one lacks.
He wants the **union** to win training for all workers, not managers only.
He respects that **Dorota** may simply retire rather than adapt.

steps.text: Start the two-year robotics certificate next autumn
Use AI tools every week for farm office records and orders
Push the baby plan back about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 when the thinking side lands, almost 40 for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this fairly, and if governments waste it, that's on them. I'd talk about it in the union, but it'd be one item on the list, not the whole meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it feels far enough that I'd mostly get on with life. I'd still want to be the robot person eventually, but not this year. The bigger question is whether I'm still on someone else's farm at 40, or on one of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working Hollin as normal and keep saving. Somewhere around 2030 I'd do the robotics course. And I'd lobby our regional council for a public farm-training fund, because they'll actually listen if a few of us turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. It's a background hum rather than a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your own farm. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a dream more than a plan. Land round here is far too expensive for a farm worker, even a well-paid one. Maybe with ten years and Sam's help, a small share in a cooperative farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your future kids to go into farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to go into farming only if they love it, and to learn to fix the machines as well as the animals. That's what I'd have told myself at 18, if I'd known.

say: I'd say a decade is time to act **fairly**, and governments must not waste it.
I'd raise it at the **union**, as one item among many.
think: Privately ten years lets me **get on with life** for now.
My bigger question is owning a **share of a farm** by 40.
do: Keep working Hollin as normal and **keep saving** each month.
Lobby the **regional council** for a public farm-training fund.
feel: He feels **quietly uneasy**, like a **background hum**.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids to go into farming only if they love it, and to learn to fix the machines as well as the animals.
fieldNote: A long horizon turns AI into a **background** concern behind land ownership.
He lowers his ambition to a **co-op share**, given land prices.
His advice to future kids blends **animal skill** and machine repair.
He prefers **local lobbying** where he thinks people listen.

steps.text: Keep running Hollin's flock and arable as normal
Lobby the regional council for a public farm-training fund
Keep saving towards a share in a cooperative farm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right when Sam and I wanted to start a family and before I've retrained. What would help is paid retraining, run publicly or through the union, and a rule that big owners like pension funds can't sack a whole farm team with a month's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. If the pension fund owns them, the money leaves the valley. If farmers own the robots together, the money stays where the work used to be.

headlineQuote: If farmers own the robots together, the money stays where the work used to be.
portrait: Victor is 27, **assistant manager** on a pension-fund-owned estate, living with Sam, a primary **teacher**.
His day splits between **fieldwork** with his team and office work he already partly hands to a **chatbot**.
He blames **absentee owners** more than technology, and joined the union after lambing cuts.
In faster scenarios he turns to **retraining** in farm robotics and delays a **baby**.
With more time he settles into **steady planning** and dreams of a co-op farm share.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits when he wants a **family** and before retraining.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** through the state or union, and limits on owners sacking teams at **short notice**.
